app.title: Rastro: Treino (training mode of the Rastro brown-dwarf candidate reviewer)
app.summary: A person works through a shuffled set of practice cases that already have known answers, with the same number of cases for each answer. Each case shows the same screen as the real review: an infrared cutout, an optical cutout and an animation of the source across epochs, plus a few numbers and an automatic checklist with a suggested call. The person answers confirm, doubt or discard. The page then shows the correct answer, why it is correct and which image held the clue, and scores the answer, with doubt worth half a point. Answers are saved to a history that reports accuracy overall, over the last 20 answers and for each correct answer, which exposes bias, and from these it gives a reviewer level.

task.text: Train and calibrate a person's visual judgement on cases with known answers before they review real candidates, and measure their accuracy and bias.

data.text: A balanced set of labelled cases. Each one has a sky position, a few catalogue measurements, crossmatch results from other catalogues, the correct decision and an explanation, plus image cutouts and an epoch-by-epoch animation fetched for that position. A history table holds one row for each answer.
data.item: a labelled practice case: one catalogue source with its images, measurements and known correct decision

stage.text: training reviewers on labelled cases before the visual vetting of candidates

mechanism.text: A queue steps through cases one at a time. For each case, three image panels sit above a stats card and a rule-based checklist, and beside them a decision panel. Once the person answers, the panel shows the correct answer, an explanation and a hint. A header bar and a history panel keep score, accuracy for each correct answer, and a level.

field.text: visual vetting of high proper-motion candidates from survey catalogues in astronomy

workflow.name: practise a keep-or-drop decision on items with known answers and track accuracy

steps.here: A shuffled set of labelled cases is drawn at random for each session, with equal numbers of each answer, and crossmatched once against other catalogues so the checklist can be filled in

steps.step: learn what to look for from good and bad examples
steps.here: An expandable guide gives one question for each image and shows a good and a bad example image, both taken from other cases in the set. The case on screen is never used as an example

An infrared cutout, an optical cutout and a GIF of yearly frames, all with a crosshair, plus a card of motion, significance, colour and magnitude, and a checklist marked with ✅/⚠️/❌ that ends in a suggested call

steps.step: decide keep or drop for each item, with a reason
steps.here: Confirm, Doubt or Discard. The panel then shows the correct answer, its explanation and where the clue was, and says whether the answer was right, half right or wrong

steps.step: step through items one at a time
steps.here: Previous/Next buttons and a 'Case i of N' counter. Restart appears on the last case

steps.step: track progress toward a target or a total
steps.here: The header shows correct answers out of answers given. The history shows accuracy overall, over the last 20 answers and for each correct answer, and a level line shows what is still needed to reach 80% over the last 20

distinctive: The decision depends on several kinds of evidence: imaging in two wavebands, plus an animation over many epochs to check that the object moves steadily

Cases are balanced across the correct answers, so always giving the most common answer does not score well. Accuracy is also split by correct answer to reveal bias, such as confirming almost everything
Doubt counts as half a point, so admitting uncertainty is rewarded more than a wrong call
After each answer the page names the image that held the clue and gives the case's own numbers
Reviewer levels depend on accuracy over the last 20 answers and on how even that accuracy is across answer classes
